article.overview: A passive seismometer is a scientific instrument designed to detect and measure ground motion without deliberately generating seismic waves. On the Moon, it is used to investigate moonquakes, meteorite impacts and the internal structure of the lunar body.
article.description: A passive seismometer is a highly sensitive instrument that measures vibrations and movements of the ground. It detects seismic waves travelling through the lunar surface and interior, converting these movements into electrical signals that can be recorded, processed and analysed. Unlike an active seismic instrument, which deliberately generates vibrations and measures their reflections, a passive seismometer simply listens for naturally occurring seismic activity. These signals can originate from moonquakes, impacts by meteoroids, thermal stresses and other geological processes. Seismometers are particularly valuable in lunar exploration because the Moon has no Earth-like global network of seismic monitoring stations. Each instrument therefore provides important information about the local environment and, when combined with other stations or historical measurements, can help scientists investigate the Moon's interior.
article.scientific_purpose_and_applications: The primary purpose of a lunar passive seismometer is to study the Moon's seismic activity and internal structure. By measuring the arrival times, amplitudes and frequencies of seismic waves, scientists can investigate the properties of materials through which those waves travel. These observations can help determine the thickness and structure of the lunar crust, investigate the mantle and provide constraints on the size and physical state of the lunar core. The instrument can also detect impacts, which provide information about the frequency and distribution of meteoroid collisions with the Moon. Seismic monitoring is also important for understanding the mechanical behaviour of the lunar surface. Repeated observations can reveal how the Moon responds to temperature changes, gravitational stresses and geological disturbances.
article.operating_principle: A passive seismometer generally contains one or more sensitive mechanical sensing elements. When the ground moves, the instrument's housing moves with it, while an internal suspended mass tends to remain relatively stationary because of inertia. The relative movement between the mass and the instrument housing is measured by a transducer. Depending on the instrument design, this movement may be converted into an electrical signal through electromagnetic, capacitive or other sensing techniques. The signal is then amplified, digitised and recorded with a precise time reference. Scientists analyse the resulting seismic waveform to determine the characteristics of the event. The time taken for seismic waves to arrive, their frequency content and their amplitude can provide information about the source and the materials through which they travelled.
article.scientific_importance: The Moon's interior cannot be investigated adequately through surface photographs or remote sensing alone. Seismic waves provide a way of studying the material beneath the surface without physically excavating it. The Apollo seismic experiments demonstrated the scientific value of this approach. The instruments detected several types of seismic events, including deep moonquakes, shallow moonquakes, meteoroid impacts and thermal moonquakes. Data from the Apollo seismic network helped scientists investigate the structure and properties of the lunar interior. A modern lunar seismic network could improve these investigations by providing more sensitive measurements, covering additional regions of the Moon and operating for longer periods.

physical_specifications.note: There is no single universal mass or size for a passive seismometer. Values below describe specific historical or proposed instruments, not every passive seismometer.

examples.name: Apollo Passive Seismic Experiment (PSE)
examples.sensor_configuration: Three matched long-period seismometers aligned orthogonally to measure one vertical and two horizontal components, plus one short-period vertical seismometer.
examples.construction: Principally beryllium, with other materials in the instrument assembly.
examples.qualification: Smithsonian documentation describes an 11.5 kg instrument including electronics and thermal insulation. NASA describes the Apollo 11 flight experiment as solar-powered, with thermal control including a radioisotope heater. The 11.5 kg instrument figure should not be confused with the mass of a complete deployment pallet or other mission-level package.

examples.power: Independent power system with a solar panel and onboard battery.

physical_specifications.dimensions_and_proportions: The Apollo instrument used a relatively compact cylindrical enclosure, whereas the Farside Seismic Suite uses a larger cube-within-a-cube package. The difference reflects changes in sensor technology, thermal management, power and communications architecture. A new seismometer would need its dimensions determined by its intended measurement range and sensitivity. In particular, the instrument must be mounted securely and isolated from disturbances that could interfere with the measurements.
physical_specifications.mass_and_weight: For spacecraft engineering, mass is normally expressed in kilograms. The payload's mass affects launch requirements, lander capacity, structural support and deployment design. The Apollo PSE's documented instrument mass of 11.5 kg and the FSS's approximate 45 kg mass illustrate how different scientific architectures can have substantially different transportation requirements.

article.environmental_and_operational_requiremen: A lunar seismometer must function in an environment that differs considerably from Earth. The Moon has no substantial atmosphere, experiences extreme surface temperature variations and is exposed to radiation and micrometeoroid impacts. The instrument therefore needs suitable thermal insulation, temperature regulation, mechanical protection and reliable electronics. It must also be installed on a stable surface so that unwanted movement of its support structure does not contaminate the seismic measurements. Mechanical vibrations from lander equipment, thermal expansion and other surface activities can affect measurements, so instrument placement and isolation are important engineering considerations.
article.limitations: A single passive seismometer can detect seismic events and record their characteristics, but it cannot always determine their exact locations or depths independently. A network of separated seismic stations provides much more information because scientists can compare the arrival times and characteristics of the same event at different locations. Measurements can also be affected by instrument noise, poor ground contact, thermal disturbances and limitations in sensor sensitivity.

transportation_and_deployment.overview: A passive seismometer can be delivered to the Moon as part of a dedicated scientific payload or as one component of a larger lunar surface experiment package.
transportation_process: Integrate the instrument into a spacecraft or lander payload compartment on Earth.
Launch it into space using a launch vehicle.
Use a lunar lander to deliver it to the surface.
Deploy and position it on a suitable support surface.
Level and thermally protect the instrument, then connect its required power and communications systems.
transportation_and_deployment.deployment_methods: Depending on its design, deployment may involve a robotic arm, a dedicated deployment mechanism or astronaut installation. The Apollo PSE was deployed by astronauts as part of the Apollo lunar surface experiment programme.
transportation_and_deployment.historical_examples: The Apollo experiments provide a historical example: astronauts transported and installed the PSE as part of the Apollo lunar surface experiment programme. The Farside Seismic Suite provides a modern example of a self-contained seismic payload designed for lunar delivery, with its own power and communications architecture.
transportation_and_deployment.compatibility_assessment: A future seismometer's compatibility with a particular lunar lander would need to be assessed using its mass, dimensions, mounting points, landing loads, deployment method, power requirements and communications architecture. It should not be assigned to a specific lander until those requirements have been compared with verified spacecraft specifications.

article.historical_significance: The Apollo 11 Passive Seismic Experiment was the first seismometer placed on the Moon. It returned data for approximately three weeks before it stopped responding, probably because of overheating during the lunar daytime. More advanced seismic stations deployed by Apollo 12, 14, 15 and 16 continued transmitting data until September 1977. Together, the later stations provided a network that recorded different types of lunar seismic events and contributed significantly to scientific understanding of the Moon's interior.
article.limitations_and_uncertainties: The payload name 'passive seismometer' describes a class of instruments rather than one standard design. The Apollo and FSS examples are not interchangeable. Values such as mass, dimensions, power, lifetime and sensor response must always be tied to a named instrument and source. The article's generic environmental and deployment discussion describes engineering considerations; it is not a certified design specification for a new payload.
